notes: Mastidia (Mâthie) is a local saint of Troyes; the inscription is quoted as Le Blanc remembers it.

sections.title: First argument: worship without God's word is will-worship
sections.pass_a: Further, that the Blessed Spirits, whether of men or of Angels, are not to be worshipped with that worship which is shown to them in the Roman Church, while namely sacred buildings and altars are constructed and dedicated in their honor, candles are lit to them, incense is burned, and before them as if looking on the knees are bent: while vows are pronounced to them, and various offerings are made to them, and oaths are conceived by their name: while finally with solemn prayers one flees to their aid and help, and hymns are publicly sung to them in thanksgiving for benefits received from God, and whatever things are of this kind: that neither the blessed Angels, I say, nor the Saints who died in Christ are to be worshipped in that way, the Protestants prove first from this, that such worship ought not to have been devised by men without the word of God. Otherwise it will be shown without faith: since without the word of God no one can be certain that it is pleasing and acceptable to God. And so if it is established that worship of this kind rests on no precept and revelation of God, it can deservedly be rejected among the will-worships condemned by the Apostle. But now that that whole worship has no foundation in the word of God is evident from this, that in the whole Scripture whether of the Old or of the New Testament, no precept of it exists, nor example.
pass_b: The Protestants hold that the blessed spirits, whether of men or of angels, are not to be honored with the worship the Roman Church gives them: churches and altars built and dedicated in their honor, candles lit to them, incense burned, knees bent before them as though they were watching; vows made to them, offerings of every kind presented, oaths sworn by their name; and, finally, solemn prayers by which people run to them for help, and hymns sung to them publicly in thanksgiving for benefits received from God, and anything else of the kind.

Neither the blessed angels, I say, nor the saints who have died in Christ are to be worshiped in this way. The Protestants prove it first from the fact that such worship ought not to have been devised by human beings apart from God's word. Otherwise it will be offered without faith, since without God's word no one can be sure that it pleases God and is accepted by him.

So if it is clear that worship of this kind rests on no command or revelation of God, it may rightly be rejected as one of the forms of self-made worship that the Apostle condemns. And it is plain that this whole worship has no foundation in God's word, since in all of Scripture, Old Testament or New, there is no command for it and no example of it.

lemmas.gloss: it will be shown (offered) without faith

choices.why: Colossians 2:23; 'self-made worship' renders the Greek compound in plain English.

sections.title: Old Testament: no worship of angels, though they ministered often to Israel
sections.pass_a: And indeed as regards the Old Testament, the Doctors of the Roman Church themselves confess that the worship which is customarily shown among them to the departed Saints was not in use in the Church of the Old Testament. Of which thing they bring this reason, that the souls of the Saints at that time did not yet enjoy that heavenly glory and blessedness, to which they were raised after the coming of Christ: but were detained in a kind of prison, which prison they call the limbo of the Fathers. But at least there is no reason why the worship which they show to Angels, if indeed it is lawful, ought not to have been shown to Angels under the Old Testament. Indeed if ever Angels are to be worshipped, then most of all they ought to have been worshipped: since in governing the ancient people God for the most part used the ministry of Angels, and their appearances were frequent in the Jewish Church: because namely God more often used them as go-betweens among the faithful. Whereas in the Church of the New Testament God has spoken to us through the Son, to whom and not to Angels he subjected this world to come, as the Apostle teaches, Hebrews 2:3 (2:5). And yet neither from sacred Scripture, nor even from any monuments of the history and of the Jewish Nation, can it be shown that even the least part of public worship was spent on Angels, for example, that any chapel or oratory was consecrated in their honor, or any feasts celebrated, and even a single candle, or grain of incense was offered and lit to them: or that in the public assemblies of the faithful any prayers were conceived to them, and hymns sung, or finally any kind of adoration shown. Indeed the contrary is plainly and undoubtedly established among all. Although nothing would have prevented it, indeed it would have been most fitting to follow Angels with such worship among the Jews, if indeed that were lawful among us.
pass_b: As for the Old Testament, the teachers of the Roman Church themselves admit that the worship they usually give to departed saints was not practiced in the Old Testament Church. The reason they give is that at that time the souls of the saints did not yet enjoy the heavenly glory and blessedness to which they were raised after Christ's coming, but were held in a kind of prison, which they call the limbo of the Fathers.

But at least there is no reason why the worship they give to angels, if it is lawful, should not have been given to angels under the Old Testament. In fact, if angels are ever to be worshiped, that was the time above all: God mostly used the ministry of angels in governing his ancient people, and they appeared frequently in the Jewish Church, because God often used them as his messengers to the faithful. In the Church of the New Testament, by contrast, God has spoken to us through the Son, to whom, and not to angels, he has subjected the world to come, as the Apostle teaches in Hebrews 2:5.

Yet neither from Holy Scripture nor from any record of the history of the Jewish nation can it be shown that even the smallest part of public worship was given to angels: that any chapel or oratory was consecrated in their honor, any feast kept, or a single candle lit or grain of incense offered to them; or that in the public assemblies of the faithful any prayers were addressed to them, hymns sung, or any form of adoration shown at all. On the contrary, everyone agrees beyond doubt that the opposite is plainly the case. And nothing would have stood in the way; indeed, it would have been most fitting for the Jews to honor angels with such worship, if it were lawful for us.

choices.why: Internuntius is a go-between; in context it names angels as God's envoys.

notes: The 1675 print reads Heb. 2. 3; the words cited are Hebrews 2:5, so the English gives 2:5.

sections.title: New Testament: Christ and the Apostles instituted no new worship of angels or saints
sections.pass_a: But under the New Testament Christ and the Apostles changed nothing at all in this part. Nor did they institute any new worship, by which thenceforth Angels and the Spirits of the Just admitted to seeing the face of God would be worshipped. For of this thing no precept, or example, or even the least indication appears in the whole Scripture of the New Testament. In which nowhere are we admonished to invoke Angels or departed Saints, to flee to their help, to sing hymns to them publicly, and to honor them with frankincense, incense, altars and sacred buildings, or any other external acts of adoration.
pass_b: Under the New Testament, Christ and the Apostles changed nothing at all in this respect. They instituted no new worship by which angels and the spirits of the righteous, admitted to the sight of God's face, were from then on to be worshiped. There is no command, no example, not even the slightest hint of it anywhere in the New Testament. Nowhere are we told there to invoke angels or departed saints, to run to them for help, to sing hymns to them publicly, or to honor them with frankincense and incense, altars and churches, or any other outward acts of adoration.

lemmas.gloss: admitted to seeing the face of God

choices.why: Echoes Hebrews 12:23, 'the spirits of just men made perfect'.

sections.title: Nor does the tradition of the first three centuries know such worship
sections.pass_a: And not only is there deep silence about those things in the writings of the New Testament, but neither can anything similar be carved out of the Ecclesiastical tradition of the first three centuries. Not a few were the illustrious writers among the Christians through that time, whose monuments survive, and which are in the hands of men. Such as among the Latins Tertullian, Cyprian, Lactantius, and Arnobius; and among the Greeks Justin, Athenagoras, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen and very many others: in whom it is nowhere read that any worship like that of today in the Roman Church was either shown formerly, or is now to be shown, to Angels and dead Saints: but the contrary is gathered from many and quite manifest indications.
pass_b: Not only is there deep silence about these things in the writings of the New Testament; nothing of the kind can be extracted from the church's tradition of the first three centuries either.

There were many distinguished Christian writers in that period whose works survive and are in people's hands: among the Latins, Tertullian, Cyprian, Lactantius, and Arnobius; among the Greeks, Justin, Athenagoras, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and many others. Nowhere in them do we read that any worship like that of the present Roman Church was once given, or is now to be given, to angels and dead saints. On the contrary, many quite obvious signs point the other way.

lemmas.gloss: are in the hands of men

choices.why: The image is of chiseling something out by force; 'extracted' keeps the sense of a forced reading.

sections.title: First sign: early writers kept the souls of the faithful outside heaven until the resurrection
sections.pass_a: For first, the Ecclesiastical writers who lived in the second and third century after Christ were for the most part of this opinion, that the souls of all the faithful, even the most holy, are held in certain places outside heaven, until the last day of judgment, and are not admitted into that heavenly homeland before the body is received back from the resurrection. Some of them indeed, from a certain singular prerogative, assign a special place to the Martyrs, namely paradise, as they call it. But by that name they by no means designate the highest heaven itself, in which the Martyrs would see the Lord face to face: but a certain subcelestial region, more joyful and more pleasant indeed than the bosom of Abraham, in which the souls of the remaining pious rest, yet not capable of heavenly glory: as John Daillé of renowned memory amply demonstrates against Cardinals Bellarmine and Perron. Whence it is evident that in those first centuries of Christianity the dogma of that worship and invocation of the Saints, which now prevails in the Roman Church, had not yet been received as Apostolic tradition. For that worship rests on the hypothesis of the highest glory and Blessedness of the Saints. To which since, according to the Roman School, the souls of the Saints were not admitted before the coming of Christ, therefore they confess that they had not yet been solemnly worshipped and invoked. On Punishments and Satisfactions, book 5, chapters 3, 4, 5 and 6. And On the Object of Religious Worship, book 3, chapter 22.
pass_b: First, most of the church writers who lived in the second and third centuries after Christ held that the souls of all believers, even the holiest, are kept in certain places outside heaven until the last day of judgment and are not admitted to the heavenly homeland until they receive their bodies back at the resurrection.

Some of them, it is true, give the martyrs a special place by a unique privilege, namely paradise, as they call it. But by that name they by no means mean the highest heaven itself, where the martyrs would see the Lord face to face. They mean a region below heaven, happier and more pleasant, indeed, than Abraham's bosom, where the souls of the other godly rest, yet not capable of heavenly glory. John Daillé, of renowned memory, shows this at length against Cardinals Bellarmine and Perron.

It follows that in those first centuries of Christianity the doctrine of the worship and invocation of saints now prevailing in the Roman Church had not yet been received as apostolic tradition. That worship rests on the assumption that the saints enjoy the highest glory and blessedness. Since, according to the Roman school, the souls of the saints were not admitted to that glory before Christ's coming, they admit that the saints were not yet solemnly worshiped and invoked. (On Punishments and Satisfactions, book 5, chapters 3 to 6; and On the Object of Religious Worship, book 3, chapter 22.)

lemmas.gloss: more joyful than the bosom of Abraham

choices.why: Echo of 1 Corinthians 13:12, kept as the familiar phrase.

sections.title: Second sign: ancient liturgies prayed for all the dead, even apostles and the Virgin
sections.pass_a: Then from the most ancient Liturgies which survive it is established that those ancient Christians offered to God prayers and supplications for absolutely all the dead, even for the most Holy, for the Martyrs, for the Apostles, and even for the Virgin Mother of God herself. For whom they ask from God in those Liturgies that he make them rest in the region of the living, and bestow on them the goods of his promises, and grant rest and good memory: and not, simply, as Bellarmine vainly contends, do they offer thanksgivings for them. But now since the Religious worship and invocation of the Saints was publicly received, that oracle of Augustine has been held as it were, He does injury to a Martyr who prays for a Martyr. Nor will anyone ever bring his mind to use that solemn invocation, which the Roman Church teaches is owed to the Saints reigning with Christ, toward those whom it is needful to commend to God by our prayers.
pass_b: Second, the oldest surviving liturgies show that those early Christians offered prayers and supplications to God for absolutely all the dead, even for the holiest, for the martyrs, for the apostles, and even for the Virgin Mother of God herself. In those liturgies they ask God to give them rest in the land of the living, to grant them the good things he has promised, and to give them rest and a good remembrance. They are not simply offering thanks for them, as Bellarmine vainly argues.

But ever since the religious worship and invocation of the saints was publicly received, Augustine's saying has been treated almost as an oracle: "He wrongs a martyr who prays for a martyr." And no one will ever bring himself to use the solemn invocation that the Roman Church teaches is owed to the saints reigning with Christ toward people who need to be commended to God by our prayers.

lemmas.gloss: in the region of the living

lemmas.latin: Injuriam facere Martyri qui orat pro Martyre
lemmas.gloss: he does injury to a Martyr who prays for a Martyr

choices.why: Standard rendering of the Latin equivalent of Theotokos.

sections.title: Third sign: against pagans the early Christians owned one God and no subordinate cult
sections.pass_a: Moreover when the wise men of the Gentiles professed that they acknowledged only one supreme God, but that the others whom they called Gods were Ministers of that one supreme deity, and were worshipped only in second place after him: and objected to the Christians that, content with the worship of that supreme God, they neglected the inferior powers under him, to whom nevertheless their own veneration also is owed: those ancient Christians in good faith acknowledged that they in truth worshipped only one supreme God, and defended this as lawful and right; nor did they concede that even the least part of religious worship was owed to the good and holy Ministers of God themselves, or distinguish religious worship into supreme and subaltern, or absolute and relative: Which nevertheless candor, charity, and prudence demanded of them, if they had held the same about the worship of Saints and Angels as the present Roman Church.
pass_b: Further, the pagan philosophers professed to acknowledge only one supreme God and said that the others they called gods were servants of that one supreme deity, worshiped only in second place after him. They charged the Christians with being content to worship the supreme God and neglecting the lesser powers under him, to whom, they said, a veneration of their own was also due.

Those early Christians frankly admitted that they did in fact worship only one supreme God, and they defended this as lawful and right. They did not grant that even the smallest part of religious worship was owed to God's good and holy servants, nor did they divide religious worship into supreme and subordinate, or absolute and relative. Yet honesty, charity, and prudence would have required exactly that of them if they had held the same view of the worship of saints and angels as the present Roman Church.

lemmas.latin: secundo solum post eum loco coli
lemmas.gloss: to be worshipped only in second place after him

choices.why: The point is that they answered candidly, without hiding a subordinate cult; 'frankly' carries that.

sections.title: Arnobius: the first God suffices; his court is honored in him without naming each
sections.pass_a: For to that accusation of the Heathen they respond thus with Arnobius. For performing the worship of divinity, the first God is enough for us, father of things and Lord, establisher and governor of all. In him we worship everything which is to be worshipped, what it is fitting to adore we adore, what demands the obedience of veneration, we merit by venerations. For since we hold the head of divinity itself, from which the divinity itself of all divine things, whatever they are, is drawn, we think it superfluous to go through the persons one by one, since we both do not know who they are and what names they have, and moreover of what number they are, we can have it neither clear, nor grasped, nor explored. Which afterwards he illustrates by that very similitude brought from the courts of princes which the Heathen use in this same matter. And, he says, as in earthly kingdoms we are compelled by no necessity to adore by name, together with the princes, those placed in royal families, but in the worship of the Kings themselves whatever is attached to them feels itself comprehended by a tacit force in the honor; in no other way whoever these gods are, whom you propose to us to exist, if they are royal offspring, and arise from the princely head, even if they receive no worships by name from us, they understand nevertheless that they are honored in common with their King, and are contained in his venerations. Arnobius, Against the Nations, book 3, beginning.
pass_b: To this pagan charge the early Christians answered with Arnobius: "For the duty of worshiping the divine, the first God is enough for us, the Father of all things and their Lord, the founder and ruler of everything. In him we worship all that is to be worshiped; we adore what it is right to adore; and what calls for the homage of veneration we honor with our veneration."

"Since we hold fast to the head of divinity itself, from which the divinity of all divine beings, whatever they are, is derived, we think it pointless to go through them person by person. We do not know who they are or what names they have, and we cannot have any clear, firm, or tested knowledge of how many of them there are."

He then illustrates this with the very comparison from princes' courts that the pagans used on this point: "In earthly kingdoms no necessity forces us to pay homage by name to the members of the royal family along with the princes. In the honor paid to the kings themselves, everything connected with them feels itself silently included. In the same way, whoever these gods are whom you set before us, if they are royal offspring sprung from the sovereign head, they understand that, even if they receive no worship from us by name, they are honored together with their king and included in the veneration given to him." (Arnobius, Against the Nations, book 3, beginning.)

lemmas.gloss: we hold the head of divinity itself

choices.why: Promereri here means to win or pay due regard; 'merit' would import a theological sense foreign to Arnobius.

sections.title: Origen: imitating the angels wins their favor; God's friends follow him as a shadow
sections.pass_a: With which agree the things which Origen teaches treating a similar argument. For to Celsus contending that one ought never indeed to fall away from the worship of God and that the soul ought to be intent on him in every work and thought, but that this does not hinder that the various powers set under God are to be appeased and propitiated, and that this redounds to the honor of the supreme deity, That distinguished Doctor of the ancient Church responds, For this, that the Angels of God be propitious to us, and do all things for us, there suffices first our affection toward God, and our disposition, as far as human nature is able, imitating the judgment of the Angels themselves who imitate God, and second the grasp of the Son of God and Word according to our strength. Likewise, One God is to be appeased by us, Lord of all things, and that we may have him propitious, he must be prayed to, who is propitiated by piety and every virtue. But if one wishes also after him, God above all, some others to be propitious, let him consider that just as when the body is moved its shadow too is moved; so when someone has the supreme God propitious, it follows that he has propitious all his friends, Angels, souls, spirits; for they perceive who are worthy of the favor of God, to whom not only do they themselves wish well; but also they join effort with those who wish to worship God, and appease him, and together with us pray and request; so that we dare to say that for men, who with firm purpose of mind choose better things, and follow them, as often as they pray to God, innumerable sacred powers pray together with them uncalled, offering themselves as companions to our frail and mortal race, and so to speak contending together, and laboring together with us in this struggle. Against Celsus book 5. Against the same Celsus book 8.
pass_b: Origen teaches the same when he deals with a similar argument. Celsus had argued that one must never fall away from the worship of God and that the soul must be intent on him in every action and thought, but that this did not prevent the various powers set under God from being appeased and won over, since this too redounds to the honor of the supreme deity.

That distinguished teacher of the ancient Church replies: "For the angels of God to be well disposed toward us and to do everything for us, it is enough, first, that we love God and that our disposition, as far as human nature can, imitates the judgment of the angels themselves, who imitate God; and second, that we lay hold of the Son of God, the Word, as far as we are able."

And again: "There is one God whom we must win over, the Lord of all things, and to have him favorable we must pray to him; he is won over by godliness and every virtue. But if anyone also wants others besides him, God above all, to be favorable, let him consider that, as the shadow moves when the body moves, so when someone has the supreme God favorable, it follows that he has all God's friends favorable too: angels, souls, and spirits."

"For they perceive who are worthy of God's favor. They not only wish such people well but also work alongside those who want to worship God; they seek his favor and pray and plead together with us. So we dare to say that whenever people who have firmly resolved to choose and follow what is better pray to God, countless holy powers pray with them uncalled, offering themselves as companions to our frail and mortal race, contending, so to speak, at our side and laboring with us in this struggle." (Against Celsus, book 5; and Against Celsus, book 8.)

lemmas.latin: moto corpore umbra quoque ipsius movetur
lemmas.gloss: when the body is moved its shadow also moves

choices.why: Origen speaks of goodwill, not atoning propitiation; 'favorable' avoids a sacrificial sense.

sections.title: Origen: prayer to God alone through the Son; invoking angels is irrational
sections.pass_a: Where it is greatly to be noted what Origen says, that innumerable sacred powers, by which name he designates the Angels and Blessed Spirits, pray together with those who wish to worship God, indeed, but uncalled, not called. For not only does he teach in general that one God is to be adored, and religiously worshipped indivisibly and inseparably, but also that our prayers are to be directed to him alone, nor is any kind of prayer and invocation to be used toward the Blessed Angels, or any other creatures whatever. Away, he says, with this counsel of Celsus bidding that daemons be prayed to (that is, Spirits who minister to the supreme God, according to the custom and usage of speaking of the Platonists) who is not to be listened to even a little. For to God Best and Greatest alone are prayers to be offered; And indeed to the only-begotten Word of God, the firstborn of all creation, are they to be offered, who as High Priest is to be asked that he carry our prayer, which reaches him, to his God and our God, his Father and our Father. In the same, against Celsus book 8. But in the fifth book of the same work, It is fitting, he says, to send forth, or carry, every supplication, and prayer, every entreaty, and thanksgiving to the supreme God, Lord of all things, through the living Word, and God, the High Priest who is above all Angels. But we shall also pray to the Word himself, and entreat him, and give thanks to him, and also offer prayers, provided we can understand the proper and the Catachrestically so called manner of praying. For that Angels be invoked by us, who have by no means received knowledge, or acquaintance, of them, a thing namely set above men, is foreign to reason. And granting that the knowledge of them, which is wonderful and secret, is grasped, this very knowledge, showing their nature, and over whom, or over what, each is set and ordered, will forbid that we dare to pray to any other than the Lord who is above all things, and who abundantly suffices for all things, through our savior the Son of God.
pass_b: Here it should be carefully noted that Origen says the countless holy powers, by which he means the angels and blessed spirits, do pray together with those who want to worship God, but uncalled, without being summoned. He teaches not only in general that one God is to be adored and religiously worshiped, undivided and inseparable, but also that our prayers are to be directed to him alone, and that no kind of prayer or invocation is to be used toward the blessed angels or any other creatures whatever.

"Away," he says, "with this advice of Celsus, who bids us pray to daemons" (that is, in the Platonists' usage, spirits who serve the supreme God); "he is not to be listened to in the least. Prayers are to be offered to God, best and greatest, alone; and also to the only-begotten Word of God, the firstborn of all creation, who as High Priest is to be asked to carry our prayer, when it reaches him, to his God and our God, his Father and our Father." (Against Celsus, book 8.)

In book 5 of the same work he says: "It is fitting to send up every supplication, prayer, entreaty, and thanksgiving to the supreme God, the Lord of all things, through the living Word and God, the High Priest who is above all angels. We will also pray to the Word himself, entreat him, give him thanks, and offer him prayers, provided we can understand the difference between prayer in the proper sense and prayer in a loose sense."

"For it is contrary to reason that angels should be invoked by us, since we have by no means received knowledge of them; that is something beyond human reach. And even granting that knowledge of them, wonderful and hidden as it is, could be grasped, that very knowledge, by showing their nature and over whom or what each of them is set and appointed, will forbid us to dare pray to anyone but the Lord who is over all and amply sufficient for all things, through our Savior, the Son of God."

choices.why: In Platonist usage the term means intermediate spirits, not devils; Le Blanc glosses it so.

sections.title: Origen: even the stars, which he thought pray to God, may not be prayed to
sections.pass_a: Here also it is to be observed that Origen, like many other Doctors of the Christian School of that age, thought that the Sun, Moon, and remaining Stars are certain rational living beings, and endowed with virtue, and illumined with the light of knowledge by that wisdom which is the brightness of eternal light: nor does he in any way resist Celsus proclaiming them, as the most illustrious heralds of higher things, and truly heavenly Angels, and he himself was fully persuaded that the Sun, Moon, and Stars offered prayers to God the Lord of all things through his only-begotten. Therefore if, in Origen's mind, the Angels of God are worthy of some worship of religion, by that it is also right that the Sun, Moon, and Stars be thought worthy. And yet when Celsus complains that the Jews do not worship the Sun, Moon, and Planets, he not only denies in general that it is right to revere and bow before those creatures, to worship and adore them; but also asserts that it is unlawful to supplicate them, and to sing hymns. We judge, he says, that it is not fitting to pray to those who themselves pray. Indeed he adds that the Sun and the stars themselves so wish, and send us back to God, to whom they themselves pray, rather than to cast us and let us down to themselves, or to divide from God that power of praying which we have, and take some part of it also for themselves. And afterwards he adds, Since the Lord is present everywhere with us and near us, it is absurd to seek to pray to him who does not reach all the way to all things, the Sun, and the Moon, or some other Star. And finally to Celsus writing that we would seem to worship the great God more by this, if we also sing hymns to the Sun, He responds that he knows the contrary. For hymns, he says, we speak to the only God, Lord of all things, and to his only-begotten God the Word. Against Celsus book 5.
pass_b: It should also be noted here that Origen, like many other teachers of the Christian school in that age, thought the sun, the moon, and the other stars were rational living beings, endowed with virtue and enlightened with the light of knowledge by the Wisdom that is the radiance of eternal light. He does not oppose Celsus at all when Celsus praises them as the most glorious heralds of things above and truly heavenly angels, and he himself was fully convinced that the sun, moon, and stars offer prayers to God, the Lord of all things, through his only-begotten Son.

So if, in Origen's view, God's angels deserve some religious worship, the sun, moon, and stars ought by the same reasoning to be thought worthy of it as well. Yet when Celsus complains that the Jews do not worship the sun, moon, and planets, Origen not only denies in general that it is right to revere and bow down to those creatures, that is, to worship and adore them; he also declares it unlawful to make supplication to them or sing hymns to them. "We judge," he says, "that it is not fitting to pray to those who themselves pray."

He adds that the sun and the stars themselves want it so: they would rather send us on to God, to whom they themselves pray, than draw us down to themselves, or split off from God the power of prayer we have and take part of it for themselves. Later he adds that since the Lord is everywhere with us and near us, it is absurd to seek to pray to something that does not reach to all things, whether the sun, the moon, or any other star.

Finally, when Celsus writes that we would seem to honor the great God more if we also sang hymns to the sun, he answers that he knows the opposite is true: "We sing hymns to the only God, the Lord of all things, and to his only-begotten, God the Word." (Against Celsus, book 5.)

sections.title: Against Perron: Origen excludes relative as well as absolute prayer to angels
sections.pass_a: Nor is there reason for anyone to say with Cardinal Perron that, when Origen denies that Angels are to be prayed to and invoked, he treats of the Prayer which they call absolute, not however of that which is called Relative, which alone the Roman School teaches is to be used toward Angels. For Celsus himself, against whom Origen acts, did not think that Angels, or as he speaks with Plato, daemons, were to be worshipped with supreme and absolute worship, but with that which would be referred to the supreme God, whose ministers they were. And so against the Christians he contended that they were to be invoked not with some absolute prayer, as if they were the first and supreme bestowers of goods, but only with relative, as obtainers and administrators of them under the supreme God. And therefore since Origen denies that they are to be invoked in the manner Celsus and other wise men of the Heathen wished, it is plain that, according to Origen, it is lawful to use neither absolute nor relative invocation toward them. Add that Origen, saying that they pray for us uncalled, not called, sufficiently indicates that they are not even to be asked to pray to God for us: which is to deny them relative prayer, and not only absolute.
pass_b: Nor can anyone say with Cardinal Perron that when Origen denies that angels are to be prayed to and invoked, he means the kind of prayer they call absolute, not the kind called relative, which is the only kind the Roman school says may be used toward angels.

Celsus himself, whom Origen is answering, did not think that angels, or daemons, as he calls them with Plato, were to be worshiped with supreme and absolute worship, but with a worship referred to the supreme God, whose servants they were. So against the Christians he argued that they should be invoked, not with absolute prayer, as if they were the first and highest givers of good things, but only with relative prayer, as those who obtain and dispense those goods under the supreme God.

Since Origen denies that they are to be invoked in the way Celsus and other pagan philosophers wanted, it is plain that, according to Origen, neither absolute nor relative invocation may be used toward them. Moreover, when Origen says they pray for us uncalled, without being summoned, he shows clearly enough that they are not even to be asked to pray to God for us. That denies them relative prayer, not merely absolute prayer.

sections.title: Origen grants angels only the honor of praise and imitation
sections.pass_a: And so Origen, struck by the objections of Celsus, as though the Christians despised the Ministers of the supreme God, and the Angelic powers, and followed them with no honor, concedes that no other honor is to be shown to them than that which consists in praise and imitation: Them, he says, we proclaim blessed, and we speak well of those to whom the interests of men have been committed by God, yet we do not render to them the honor owed to God. In the often already cited eighth book against Celsus the Philosopher. And moreover in the place which we described above from the fifth book of the same work, he affirms that the Angels, as far as human nature allows, are to be imitated by us; and that this will be enough for those blessed Spirits to wish us well, and to busy themselves for us in all things: but nowhere, which nevertheless would have served his purpose most, and would have beaten back the calumny of the Heathen still more fully, does he mention that we court their prayers with our prayers, or that anything of those things which are in use today in the Roman Church is done in their honor.
pass_b: So Origen, pressed by Celsus's objections that Christians despised the servants of the supreme God and the angelic powers and gave them no honor at all, grants that no other honor is to be given them than the honor that consists in praise and imitation. "We call them blessed," he says, "and we speak well of those to whom God has entrusted the welfare of human beings, yet we do not give them the honor owed to God." (Against Celsus the Philosopher, book 8, cited several times already.)

In the passage from book 5 of the same work quoted above, he also states that we are to imitate the angels as far as human nature allows, and that this will be enough for those blessed spirits to wish us well and to take pains for us in everything. But nowhere does he mention that we solicit their prayers by praying to them, or that any of the things used in the Roman Church today are done in their honor, though that would have served his purpose best and would have refuted the pagan slander even more fully.

sections.title: Origen's therapeia toward Gabriel and Michael is acknowledgment and imitation, not invocation
sections.pass_a: Therefore when Origen in that eighth book against Celsus insinuates that a certain therapeia, that is, a kind of honor and observance, is owed to the true Ministers of God, Gabriel, Michael, and the other Angels and Archangels, that therapeia, according to the doctrine of Origen, can in no way be placed in some adoration of them, and invocation, which he contends is owed wholly and indivisibly to the one supreme God: but in that acknowledgment and celebration of blessedness, glory and holiness, and also the pious imitation of obedience and love toward God, by which he confesses that we can honor the Holy Angels.
pass_b: So when Origen, in that eighth book against Celsus, suggests that a certain therapeia, that is, a kind of honor and respect, is owed to God's true servants, Gabriel, Michael, and the other angels and archangels, that therapeia, by Origen's own teaching, can in no way consist in adoring or invoking them, which he insists is owed entirely and undivided to the one supreme God. It consists in acknowledging and celebrating their blessedness, glory, and holiness, and in devoutly imitating their obedience and love toward God. These are the ways in which he admits we may honor the holy angels.
